bullets: **Tennyson was Poet Laureate** (from 1850), the official national poet. He wrote the poem within weeks after reading a report in The Times by **William Howard Russell**, one of the first modern war correspondents.
The phrase ‘some hideous blunder’ in The Times inspired the line about someone having blundered.
Newspapers and the telegraph meant that the public learned of the disaster quickly; the poem turned a military fiasco into a story of national pride.
Victorian values: **duty, obedience, patriotism, the honour of the officer class**. The poem reflects and reinforces these.
Copies were later printed and sent to soldiers in the Crimea to boost morale.

callouts.p: Link context to a choice in the poem: because Tennyson was Poet Laureate, he blames a vague ‘someone’ rather than named aristocratic officers, and turns the poem into a call to ‘honour’ the dead.

core.p: During the **Crimean War** (1853–56), Britain, France and Turkey fought Russia. At the **Battle of Balaclava** a confused order, passed from Lord Raglan through Lord Lucan to Lord Cardigan, sent the Light Brigade (light cavalry, about 600–670 men) straight down a valley lined with Russian artillery on three sides. They reached the guns, fought, and retreated; around 110 were killed and around 160 wounded, and many horses died.

bullets: **Conflict type**: military conflict seen from a distance, as a public, collective event.
**Big message**: heroic obedience and sacrifice deserve glory; leaders’ mistakes are acknowledged but not dwelt on.
**Perspective**: third-person narrator, like a ballad or a newsreel. We never hear an individual soldier.
core.p: An anonymous order sends the brigade down the ‘valley of Death’. The men know it is a mistake but obey. Surrounded by cannon, they charge, fight with sabres, break the Russian line, and ride back with heavy losses. The final stanza commands the reader to honour them.

bullets: **Refrain** ‘Rode the six hundred’ changes: ‘Not the six hundred’, then ‘Left of six hundred’, then ‘Noble six hundred’. The changing refrain is the poem’s way of counting the dead without numbers.
**Mirror structure**: stanzas 3 and 5 repeat each other with ‘in front of’ swapped for ‘behind’, like the journey down and back up the valley.
Irregular stanza lengths suggest the chaos of battle.
**Rhyme** is frequent but irregular (repeated triples like ‘bare / air / there’), adding energy and a song-like quality suitable for public recitation.
The shortest stanza at the end works like a monument inscription.
core.p: Six stanzas of varying length with a **ballad-like** narrative and a strong **dactylic** metre that imitates galloping. The stanzas track the charge: order, blunder, advance, fighting, retreat, tribute.

bullets: War is **glorious and noble**: the language of honour, glory and nobility frames the deaths as worthwhile.
War is **mechanical and overwhelming**: cannon ‘volleyed and thundered’ from every side; individual men disappear into the collective.
**Duty over reason**: ‘Theirs not to reason why’ celebrates obedience, but a modern reader may hear tragic irony.
**Leadership failure** is admitted but softened: ‘someone had blundered’.
**Remembrance** is a duty for the reader: the imperatives make the poem a memorial.

callouts.p: Patriotic reading: a celebration of courage that comforted a grieving nation. Critical reading: the poem cannot hide the waste: the vague blame, the shrinking refrain and the ambiguous ‘wild’ hint at the senselessness of the charge.

plan: Sound: galloping dactyls vs slow half-rhymes
essays.q: Compare how the deaths of soldiers are presented in The Charge of the Light Brigade and Exposure.
essays.text: Tennyson presents death as an honourable destination. The soldiers ride ‘into the valley of Death’, and the biblical echo of Psalm 23 gives their sacrifice a religious dignity; even when the refrain collapses to ‘Not the six hundred’, the losses are never counted or described, so the deaths remain heroic rather than horrific. This distance reflects Tennyson’s position as Poet Laureate writing from a newspaper report: his task was to console a nation. Owen, writing from the trenches, refuses that comfort. His soldiers use the collective ‘we’, so the reader is inside the group, and death comes not in a charge but through the cold, which ‘knive[s]’ them. Where Tennyson’s galloping dactyls drive the men forward, Owen’s long, slow lines and pararhymes such as ‘wire’ and ‘war’ seem to stall, and the refrain ‘But nothing happens’ suggests that their deaths achieve nothing. Both poems end with the dead, but Tennyson commands us to ‘Honour’ them, while Owen leaves the burying-party pausing over faces in which ‘All their eyes are ice’, an image that denies the reader any glory to cling to.
essays.thesis: Tennyson turns death into glory by keeping the reader at a distance, while Owen removes that distance and presents death as slow, meaningless and unseen.

mistakes.r: He did not; he wrote from a newspaper report, which explains the distant, public perspective.
mistakes.w: Tennyson fought in the Crimean War.

mistakes.r: Mainly it celebrates courage; argue that critical undertones exist (‘blundered’, ‘wild’) but do not claim it is a protest poem.
Most survived; around 110 were killed. The refrain implies loss without numbers.
Say which repetition and its effect: the changing refrain counts the dead; the anaphora traps the men.
It is mainly dactylic (stressed + two unstressed), which imitates galloping.

poem.how: Read each stanza aloud: the galloping rhythm is part of the meaning.

stanzas.label: Stanza 1: the order
lines: Half a league, half a league,
All in the valley of Death
Charge for the guns!” he said.

notes.n: **Dactylic dimeter** (DUM-da-da DUM-da-da) imitates the sound of galloping hooves. The **repetition** creates relentless forward motion: there is no turning back. A league is about three miles, so half a league is roughly a mile and a half.
notes.w: Half a league, half a league,

notes.n: **Biblical allusion** to Psalm 23 (‘the valley of the shadow of death’). Death is capitalised and personified as a place: the men ride into it knowingly. Also gives the charge a religious, sacrificial dignity.
The men are a collective, **‘the six hundred’**, never individuals. This honours their unity but also hides their individual humanity. The line becomes a **refrain** that changes later.
**Direct speech** of the commander: imperative verbs (‘Forward’, ‘Charge’) show military authority and obedience. The speaker is anonymous (‘he said’): the blame is not pinned on a named person.

stanzas.label: Stanza 2: the blunder
lines: Theirs but to do and die.

notes.n: **Rhetorical question** answered at once: no. Tennyson praises their courage and steadiness.

The only open criticism in the poem. ‘Someone’ is deliberately **vague**: Tennyson, as Poet Laureate, acknowledges the mistake without naming or attacking the commanders (Lucan, Cardigan, Raglan). The understatement makes the waste quietly shocking.
**Anaphora/tricolon**: ‘Theirs not… Theirs not… Theirs but’. The repetition sounds like a military rule recited. It presents unquestioning **duty** as noble.

The **alliteration** of ‘do and die’ makes death sound inevitable and almost simple. Readers today often read this line with irony: is blind obedience admirable or tragic? Discuss both views for a grade 9.
notes.w: Theirs but to do and die.

stanzas.label: Stanza 3: into the guns
lines: Stormed at with shot and shell,

notes.n: **Anaphora** across three lines surrounds the men on all sides, trapping them: the structure enacts the encirclement.
**Onomatopoeia** and a storm metaphor: the guns sound like natural forces, overwhelming and deafening.
**Sibilance and alliteration** (‘shot and shell’) recreate the hiss and crash of fire.
notes.w: Stormed at with shot and shell,

notes.n: Admiring **adverbs**: courage and skill persist under fire. Tennyson’s focus stays on heroism, not on suffering.
**Personification** of Death as a monster swallowing them; ‘mouth of hell’ intensifies the image from the valley in stanza 1. The language escalates as they get closer.

stanzas.label: Stanza 4: the fighting
lines: Flashed as they turned in air
Right through the line they broke;
Then they rode back, but not

notes.n: Visual image of light on swords: glamorous, almost cinematic. **Triple rhyme** (bare / air / there) speeds up the action. Note the contrast: swords against cannon shows the hopeless odds.
**Hyperbole**: the whole world watches in awe. Raises the charge to legendary status. Repeated in stanza 6.
The enemy is named only as groups and is shown reeling: the one moment of British success is emphasised.
**Alliteration** and violent past participles show the force of the attack.
The **longest stanza** and the turning point. The **enjambment** and the repeated ‘not / Not’ create a stumbling pause: the refrain has broken, just as the brigade has.
notes.w: Then they rode back, but not

notes.n: The refrain is **altered** for the first time: losses are implied, not counted. Restraint creates grief.

stanzas.label: Stanza 5: the return
lines: Stormed at with shot and shell,
They that had fought so well
Came through the jaws of Death,
Back from the mouth of hell,
All that was left of them,

notes.n: A **mirror** of stanza 3 with one change: ‘behind’ replaces ‘in front of’. The structure shows the retreat and the cyclical horror of the same guns.
**Alliteration** links animals and men; ‘hero’ keeps the glorifying tone even in death.
‘Into’ has become ‘through’ and ‘back from’: survival, but hell has been passed through, not avoided.
notes.w: Came through the jaws of Death,

notes.n: The refrain shrinks again: ‘Left of six hundred’. The repeated word ‘left’ stresses the loss without giving a number (about 110 were killed and many more wounded).
notes.w: All that was left of them,

stanzas.label: Stanza 6: the tribute
lines: O the wild charge they made!

notes.n: **Rhetorical question** implying never: the poem itself is the memorial that keeps their glory alive.
‘Wild’ is ambiguous: brave and spirited, or reckless and insane? A good place for an alternative interpretation.
notes.w: O the wild charge they made!

notes.n: **Imperatives** directly command the reader to honour them: the poem ends as a public act of remembrance and patriotic propaganda.
The final refrain restores the full number with the epithet ‘Noble’: the dead are included in the glory. The **shortest stanza** ends like a salute.

quotes.a: Biblical allusion and personification; the men knowingly enter death.
Vague blame: the mistake is admitted but the officers protected.
quotes.c: Poet Laureate; Russell’s report in The Times

quotes.a: Unquestioning obedience presented as noble duty; can be read ironically.
Guns as a natural storm: overwhelming force.
The broken refrain shows losses without numbers.
Imperative command: poem as memorial and propaganda.

summary: The Charge of the Light Brigade (1854) is Tennyson’s six-stanza tribute to 600 British cavalrymen who charged Russian guns after a mistaken order at Balaclava in the Crimean War; you must be able to compare how it presents duty, sacrifice, heroism and the blunders of leaders, with context about Tennyson as Poet Laureate.

terms.d: A metrical foot of one stressed and two unstressed syllables (HALF-a-league); creates a galloping rhythm.
A repeated line; here it changes to track the losses.
Repetition at the start of lines (‘Cannon to…’, ‘Theirs not…’).
A narrative poem with strong rhythm and repetition, often for public performance.
The monarch’s official poet, expected to write about national events.
Giving human or animal qualities to a non-human thing (Death with ‘jaws’).
